title: Cyclic perfect difference sets exist only for prime-power orders
credit: Folklore conjecture going back to Singer (1938) and Hall (1947); standard formulation in Jungnickel's and Beth–Jungnickel–Lenz's design theory texts; asymptotic version by S. Peluse.
premise_risks: Well-known problem (lower novelty); 'prime power conjecture' is not person-named but is related to famous projective-plane questions
Must be kept distinct from pending J14 (projective plane of order 12)
plain: A perfect (planar) difference set of order n is a set of n+1 residues modulo n^2+n+1 such that every nonzero residue is the difference of exactly one ordered pair of its elements. Singer showed that one exists whenever n is a prime power, and each one gives a projective plane of order n with a cyclic symmetry. Prove that if such a set exists then n is a prime power.
math: Let $n\ge2$. Suppose $D\subseteq\mathbb{Z}/(n^2+n+1)\mathbb{Z}$ has $|D|=n+1$ and that for every $x\neq0$ there is exactly one pair $(a,b)\in D\times D$ with $a-b=x$. Prove that $n$ is a prime power.
